query: Consider the following context: Non-equiatomic high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are promising candidates for low-dimensional magnetocaloric applications. In that context, which method can be used for tuning the magnetic and magnetocaloric behavior, and why?

generation.hypothesis: If the ratios of constituent elements in a non-equiatomic transition-metal-based HEA are systematically changed (e.g., partial substitution of Fe with Mn), then the Curie temperature and magnetocaloric response will shift, producing a measurable enhancement in magnetocaloric performance compared to the baseline alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline non-equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi-type high-entropy alloy showing a single-phase solution.
generation.intervention: Incrementally vary the elemental ratios (especially Fe and Mn) through controlled doping during alloy synthesis (arc or induction melting) and standard annealing conditions.
generation.conditions: Use standard melting and homogenization protocols to ensure consistent microstructures and to isolate the effect of composition variation on magnetic behavior.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical environment changes and altered magnetic interaction pathways from partial substitution of specific elements.
generation.mechanism: Adjusting elemental compositions modifies overall electron concentration and exchange interactions, shifting the magnetic transition temperature and thereby tuning the magnetocaloric response near the Curie region.
generation.predicted_outcome: A modest but discernible shift in the Curie temperature and an improved peak magnetocaloric effect relative to the undoped reference alloy.
generation.baseline: A baseline HEA composition with known magnetic transition temperature and magnetocaloric performance metrics.
generation.boundary: The doping levels must remain within the solubility range to suppress unwanted secondary phases that might degrade magnetic or structural properties.
generation.uncertainty: Precise quantitative changes of the Curie temperature and magnetocaloric effect will require empirical verification, as the specific outcomes depend on subtle phase stability and mixing effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize multiple alloy variances with systematically increasing Mn (or alternative constituent) content and measure their magnetic and caloric properties under identical processing conditions to compare performance directly.
measurements: X-ray diffraction for phase identification and fraction
Magnetization vs temperature measurements to locate Curie temperature
Isothermal magnetization experiments near the Curie temperature to assess magnetocaloric effect (ΔS, ΔT)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If doping does not change the magnetic transition temperature or fails to produce any measurable enhancement in the magnetocaloric effect compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: “Superalloy” is the general name given to iron-based, nickel-based, and cobalt-based alloys, given their high endurance, creep, and fatigue strength at high temperature. They are widely used in aviation, aerospace, and automotive and chemical industries, serving in high-temperature (≤ 1100 °C) environments. However, for super high temperature conditions of up to 1500 °C and 3000 °C, traditional surperalloys are powerless. Instead, a new type of refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have shown their advantages. High-entropy alloys or multi-element alloys are loosely defined as solid-solution alloys that contain more than five principal elements in equal or near equal atomic percent (at%) [ [1] , [2] , [3] ]. HEAs usually have unexpected properties, such as high strength, high hardness, excellent softening resistance, and wear and corrosion resistance [ [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] ]. According to the cocktail effects of HEAs, the alloy properties can be adjusted by composition changes and via alloying [ [4] , [5] , [10] ].
